known_divergences.reason: `--build-configuration` describes succinctly's build, not jq's configure line.
succinctly has no bytecode to disassemble; the flag is rejected (exit 2).
succinctly has no bytecode to trace; the flag is rejected (exit 2).
`-h` prints succinctly's own usage text.
`--help` prints succinctly's own usage text.

`"11:30 PM" | strptime("%I:%M %p")`: the weekday (element 6) is 6 in jq 1.7.1 on macOS and 0 in succinctly. It is the platform libc's weekday and yearday of a format that sets no date (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, "`strptime` weekday and yearday of a format that sets no date", #5340, #5383): jq's macOS build derives it from the unset date (`1900-01-00`) with its own `set_tm_wday()`, glibc leaves jq's `8`/`367` sentinels, and succinctly answers the date's own weekday. `"12"|strptime("%H")` and `"3"|strptime("%d")` differ the same way.

Same platform-dependent weekday as `locale-strptime-ampm-c`, under `de_DE.UTF-8`, on a host without that locale (it falls back to `C`). A host that has the locale matches: neither tool parses `PM` there, and both exit 5.
Same platform-dependent weekday as `locale-strptime-ampm-c`, under `en_US.UTF-8`.

Same platform-dependent weekday as `locale-strptime-ampm-c`, under `tr_TR.UTF-8`, on a host without that locale (it falls back to `C`). A host that has the locale matches: neither tool parses `PM` there, and both exit 5.

`"Thursday, March 05 2015" | strptime("%A, %B %d %Y")` under `de_DE.UTF-8`: glibc's `strptime` reads the `C` locale's English names as well as the locale's own, so a glibc jq 1.7.1 answers where the macOS pin's libc and succinctly exit 5 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, "glibc `jq` under a locale, measured"). Only a Linux host that has `de_DE` shows it: without the locale both tools fall back to `C` and agree.

`"Thursday, March 05 2015" | strptime("%A, %B %d %Y")` under `tr_TR.UTF-8`: the same glibc behaviour as `locale-strptime-en-de-de`, reading the `C` locale's English names beside the locale's own. Only a Linux host that has `tr_TR` shows it.

`[-101,0,1,0,0,0,0,0] | strftime("%y|%C")` is `01|-1` in jq 1.7.1 on macOS and succinctly follows it; a glibc jq prints `99|-2` (the floored remainder and quotient). Same cause as `strftime-negative-year-y`.

`[-5,0,1,0,0,0,0,0] | strftime("%y|%C|%D")` is `05|-0|01/01/05` in jq 1.7.1 on macOS (the libc's `_yconv`: the remainder's absolute value, and `-0` for a century of 0) and succinctly follows it. A glibc jq prints `95|-1|01/01/95` (the floored remainder and quotient), as it prints `%Y` of year -5 as `-5` where the pin prints `-005` (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, "negative years"). Measured on Ubuntu 22.04 with a source-built jq 1.7.1.
`--version` names the tool (`succinctly jq ... 0.8.0`), not jq's version token.
Prints the directory of the running binary, so the two tools differ by installation path alone.
Same jq 1.7.1 assertion abort on a non-string format as strftime/1.
jq 1.7.1 aborts (`Assertion failed: JVP_HAS_KIND(j, JV_KIND_STRING)`, jv.c:1370) on a non-string format; succinctly reports a catchable error.
On `"a" | strptime(.)` the weekday of 1900-00-00 is 6 in jq 1.7.1 on macOS, `[…,8,367]` on glibc, and `[…,0,-1]` in succinctly; the value is platform-libc dependent (#5340).
`[] | .[1e12] = 1`: jq aborts (SIGSEGV); succinctly refuses the index with an error (exit 5, #5500).
Under `ulimit -v` 64 MiB, 1M-integer array: the reference jq 1.7.1 aborts; succinctly answers, on an evaluation stack sized to the cap (#5634).

Under `ulimit -v` 64 MiB a 20 MB string is read by jq but aborts succinctly on a failed allocation. A trivial run already maps about 42 MiB (the binary, the main thread's 8 MiB stack and the evaluation stack, 16 MiB at the least under a cap, #5634), and the document takes 28 MiB more: the input, and its index in two allocations of 2.5 MB and 5 MB. That is the semi-index kept whole beside the input, not a leak: it fits in 70 MiB on Linux aarch64.
Under `ulimit -v` 64 MiB, 300000-key object: the reference jq 1.7.1 aborts; succinctly answers, on an evaluation stack sized to the cap (#5634).

`[range(1e8)] | length` under `ulimit -v` 512 MiB: jq 1.7.1 and succinctly both abort (killed by a signal, no exit status). Rust ends the process on a failed allocation (`memory allocation of N bytes failed`) where jq's `jv_mem_alloc` prints `cannot allocate memory` and aborts, so the output matches; a graceful error would need every container growth to be fallible.
`"a" * 1e9` under `ulimit -v` 512 MiB: jq 1.7.1 aborts; succinctly exits 5 with a graceful error.
A user-defined function recursing 10000 deep: jq answers (about 3 s); succinctly's stack guard refuses with `exceeded maximum recursion depth` (ADR-0025).
Recursion 100000 deep: jq does not finish within 10 s; succinctly's stack guard refuses (ADR-0025).
Tail-position recursion 100000 deep: jq does not finish within 10 s; succinctly's stack guard refuses (ADR-0025), so it gets no tail-call elimination.
`gsub("a";"b")` over 100000 characters: jq 1.7.1 does not finish within 10 s; succinctly answers in tens of milliseconds.

`[match("a";"g")]` over 100000 characters: jq 1.7.1 does not finish within 10 s on an M4 Pro (5.7 s on a 7950X); succinctly answers in tens of milliseconds. Whether jq beats the deadline depends on the host (it timed out on an M4 Pro and on a GitHub-hosted x86_64 Linux runner, #5565).
